title: Design a Vending Machine (OOD)
oneLiner: The State pattern question: coins, selection, change, cancel and jams, with each state's rules in one class.
keyTakeaway: A vending machine is a state machine, and the State pattern keeps each state's rules in one class instead of a switch in every method. Hold the customer's coins in escrow so cancel always works, and plan change before dispensing but only commit it after the product drops.
explanation:
Same format as the other OOD walk-throughs: write your answer for each stage first, then compare and tick what you covered. The parking lot walk-through explains what an OOD round grades.

What's specific to the vending machine. Interviewers pick it to see whether you recognise a state machine and can say why the State pattern helps: the same input (a coin, a button) means something different when the machine is idle, has credit, is dispensing or is out of service. Without the pattern each public method grows a switch over the state, and adding a state means editing all of them. With it, each state is a small class and a new state is a new class. Be ready to say what the pattern costs too: more classes, and states that need access to the machine's internals.

The other depth is money. What happens when the machine can't make change? What does cancel give back? What if the product jams after payment? The model answer keeps inserted coins in escrow, which makes refunds trivial, and shows why greedy change making can fail when the machine is short of some coins. Those details separate a pattern recital from a design that would work.
